Optimal control over 120 days: cisplatin and fasting

Generated 2026-10-06 16:16 by run_control_fasting.jl and control_fasting_report.jl. Model-predictive control now chooses two things at every media change (every 2 days) for 120 days: the cisplatin dose and whether the next 2 days are run in low resource ("fasting", 0.5% FBS). The goal is the same as in the 14-day report: a low total tumour burden with resistant cells held back (a resistant cell counts as two). Fasting has a host cost (body weight, with the cancer-cachexia threshold as a limit) and a host benefit (protection of healthy tissue from the drug), both taken from the fasting-and-chemotherapy literature. The look-ahead is 14 days, re-planned every 2 days. Scenarios A and B are as in the 14-day report.

Key findings (50:50 start)

  • Scenario A. MPC with fasting ends at 58 cells (5 resistant) vs 3932 (3926) for MPC without fasting and 3933 (3933) for constant 1 µM; it fasts on days 0–2, 26–28, 66–68, 106–108 (8 days in total), gives 126.2 µM·d of cisplatin, and keeps weight ≥ 0.975 and toxicity ≤ 0.077.
  • Scenario B. MPC with fasting ends at 50 cells (22 resistant) vs 57 (57) for MPC without fasting and 1044 (1034) for constant 1 µM; it fasts on days 0–2 (2 days in total), gives 105.2 µM·d of cisplatin, and keeps weight ≥ 0.976 and toxicity ≤ 0.077.

These results rest on how slowly starvation damage in A2780cis fades after refeeding, which was never measured (see How much rests on recovery after refeeding): if it fades in about a day and a half (k_off = 2/day), the scenario-A MPC plan ends with 3928 resistant cells instead of 5, and re-optimising gives 220 with 22 fasting days.

Read first. Days 14–120 are beyond the data (shaded on every plot). The tumour-side effect of fasting is the in-vitro serum-starvation effect at full strength, with no in-vivo attenuation yet, so fasting's benefit is an upper bound. The host states are literature-based proxies, not measurements. These are model simulations; no schedule here has been tested.

The model the controller uses

Two controls, each held constant over a 2-day interval between media changes: the cisplatin concentration \(u\) (µM) and fasting \(v\) (1 = the interval is run in 0.5% FBS, 0 = fed, 10% FBS). Fasting enters the cells through the fitted low-resource level \(u_R = 0.9547738693467337\,v\), and the host through the weight and protection states. When \(v = 0\) the model is exactly the 14-day control model; with \(u = 1\) µM and \(v = 1\) it is exactly the fitted Stage 4 model (both checked below).

Cells (scenario A; generated from the plant, with \(D = u\))

\[\frac{dN}{dt}=r_{N}\,N\left(1-\frac{N+\alpha_{NC}C}{\frac{K}{1+c_{N}\varepsilon_{N}\,u_R}}\right)-\left(1-\frac{N+\alpha_{NC}C}{\frac{K}{1+c_{N}\varepsilon_{N}\,u_R}}\right)\left[\beta_{N}\,A_{N,3}\,N\right]\]
\[\frac{dA_{N,1}}{dt}=k_{N}\left(D-A_{N,1}\right),\ \frac{dA_{N,j}}{dt}=k_{N}\left(A_{N,j-1}-A_{N,j}\right),\ j=2,\dots,3\]
\[\frac{dC}{dt}=r_{C}\,C\left[1-\left(\frac{C+\alpha_{CN}N}{K}\right)^{\theta_{C}}\right]-\left[1-\left(\frac{C+\alpha_{CN}N}{K}\right)^{\theta_{C}}\right]\left[\beta_{C}\,A_{C,3}\,C\right]-\left(d_{C}^{LR}\varepsilon_{C}\,u_R+d_{C}^{acc}S_{C,3}\right)C\]
\[\frac{dA_{C,1}}{dt}=k_{C}\left(D-A_{C,1}\right),\ \frac{dA_{C,j}}{dt}=k_{C}\left(A_{C,j-1}-A_{C,j}\right),\ j=2,\dots,3\]
\[\frac{dS_{C,1}}{dt}=k_{C}^{R}\left(\varepsilon_{C}\,u_R-S_{C,1}\right),\ \frac{dS_{C,j}}{dt}=k_{C}^{R}\left(S_{C,j-1}-S_{C,j}\right),\ j=2,\dots,3\]
\[\frac{dA_{X,1}}{dt}=k_X\,(u-A_{X,1}),\quad \frac{dA_{X,j}}{dt}=k_X\,(A_{X,j-1}-A_{X,j}),\ j=2,3,\qquad E_X=A_{X,3}\]
\[\frac{dS_{C,1}}{dt}=k_C^R\left(\varepsilon_C(u)\,u_R-S_{C,1}\right),\quad \frac{dS_{C,j}}{dt}=k_C^R\,(S_{C,j-1}-S_{C,j}),\ j=2,3\]
\[\varepsilon_X(u)=1+\left(\varepsilon_X^{S4}-1\right)\min\!\left(\frac{u}{1\,\mu\mathrm{M}},\,1\right)\]

Host

\[\frac{dB}{dt}=s_B\,u-d_B\,B\]
\[\frac{dT}{dt}=a_H\,\left(1-p_H\,P\right)\left(1-e^{-B}\right)(1-T)-r_H\,T\,(1-T)\]
\[\frac{dP}{dt}=k_P\,(v-P)\]
\[\frac{dW}{dt}=-k_W\,v+r_W\,(1-W)(1-v)\]

Objective (minimised over the look-ahead at every decision)

\[\ell=q_B\,\tfrac{N+C}{K}+q_R\,\tfrac{C}{K}+q_T\Big(\tfrac{T}{B_{tox}}\Big)^2+q_W\Big(\tfrac{1-W}{1-W_{min}}\Big)^2+r_u\Big(\tfrac{u}{u_{max}}\Big)^2+r_v\,v^2\]
\[+\,b_{\mu}\!\Big(1-\tfrac{N+C}{B_{cancer}}\Big)+b_{\mu}\!\Big(1-\tfrac{T}{B_{tox}}\Big)+b_{\mu}\!\Big(1-\tfrac{1-W}{1-W_{min}}\Big),\qquad b_\mu(z)=\begin{cases}-\mu\log z,&z\ge\delta\\ \mu\big[\tfrac12\big(\tfrac{z-2\delta}{\delta}\big)^2-\tfrac12-\log\delta\big],&z<\delta\end{cases}\]
\[J=\sum_{k=1}^{H}\ell(x_{k+1},u_k,v_k)+5\Big[q_B\,\tfrac{N+C}{K}+q_R\,\tfrac{C}{K}+q_T\Big(\tfrac{T}{B_{tox}}\Big)^2+q_W\Big(\tfrac{1-W}{1-W_{min}}\Big)^2\Big]_{H+1}\]
\[u_k\in\{0,\,0.62,\,1,\,1.47\}\ \mu\mathrm{M},\quad v_k\in\{0,1\},\quad \text{at most 1 fasting interval in a row (48 h)},\quad \ge 1\ \text{fed interval between fasts}\]

Checks against the measured low-resource conditions

  • Low resource + 1 µM cisplatin (Stage 4): the plant with u = 1 µM, v = 1 reproduces the fitted Stage 4 model to 1.2e-06 (relative).
  • Fed: with v = 0 the plant is exactly the 14-day control model (tested to 10⁻¹²).
  • Low resource alone (six low-resource cocultures, no drug, predicted with no refit): RMSE 760 cells with the dose-dependent strength ε(u) used here, versus 1499 if the Stage 4 strength were used at every dose, and 3 for the Stage 3b model fitted to these data. The controller's model is therefore less accurate than the dedicated low-resource fit for fasting without drug (it keeps the Stage 3a crowding coefficients rather than the Stage 3b ones) but far better than ignoring the drug × low-resource interaction.

How much rests on recovery after refeeding

In the fitted low-resource model (Stage 2a), starvation stress in A2780cis builds up through a three-compartment chain at rate \(k_C^R = 0.1892\)/day, and after refeeding it fades at the same slow rate (about 16 days). One 48-h fast therefore keeps killing resistant cells for weeks, which is why the controller needs so little fasting. No experiment measured recovery after refeeding: every low-resource culture stayed in 0.5% FBS for all 14 days, and the stress-death coefficient is poorly identified (flat profile likelihood). Here the stress is allowed to fade faster once fed, \(dS_{C,1}/dt = k\,(\varepsilon_C u_R - S_{C,1})\) with \(k = k_C^R\,v + k_{off}(1-v)\), and the same schedules are replayed and re-optimised.

Experiment that would settle it: A2780cis (and a 1:1 coculture) in 0.5% FBS for 48 h, then back to 10% FBS, counted daily for 10–14 days.

Tests

  • Fed (v = 0) reproduces the 14-day control model exactly; u = 1 µM with v = 1 reproduces the fitted Stage 4 model.
  • The fast, type-stable right-hand side used by the controller equals the zoo's generic right-hand side to 10⁻¹².
  • Fixed-step RK4 matches an adaptive Tsit5 solve; automatic-differentiation Jacobians A = ∂F/∂x and B = ∂F/∂(u, v) match central finite differences; the adjoint gradient matches finite differences of the cost.
  • The exact search equals brute force with the fasting rules, and a warm start never changes its answer; SQP keeps both controls in bounds and never raises the cost.
  • Weight, protection and toxicity follow their equations; with p_H = 0 fasting gives no protection.

Run test/test_control_fasting.jl.

What the data do not support

  • No in-vivo attenuation yet. The tumour-side effect of fasting is the in-vitro effect of 0.5% FBS at full strength. A patient's fast changes serum glucose, insulin and IGF-1 far less than a 20-fold serum cut, so the benefit shown here is an upper bound. Scaling it down is the planned next step.
  • Recovery after refeeding of starvation damage was never measured, and the result depends on it strongly (section above).
  • Days 14–120 extrapolate every stage beyond the data. The model has no passaging: a culture near its capacity K stays there, which no real culture does for 120 days, so read the late days as the long-run tendency of the fitted equations, not as a prediction for a flask.
  • Fasting without drug is predicted less accurately than by the dedicated Stage 3b fit (checks above), and the drug × low-resource interaction was measured at one dose only (1 µM).
  • Host states are literature-informed proxies: nothing in these experiments measured toxicity, weight or protection. The weight rates come from a case series, the cachexia threshold from a consensus definition, and the protection strength is an assumption (the randomized DIRECT trial found less DNA damage in T cells but no difference in toxicity grades, so p_H = 0 is in the sweep).
  • Resistant kill in coculture (scenario A vs B) remains the largest structural uncertainty, as in the 14-day report. Scenario A passes leave-one-ratio-out validation but was fitted to the treated cocultures; only scenario B was tested on held-out treated cocultures.
  • The toxicity limit is inactive at the default settings. T can never exceed a_H/r_H = 0.1 (less while fasting protects healthy tissue), below the bound B_tox = 0.25; the toxicity cost still discourages dosing, but the hard limit never decides a schedule here.

References

  • Raffaghello L et al. (2008). Starvation-dependent differential stress resistance protects normal but not cancer cells against high-dose chemotherapy. PNAS 105:8215–8220.
  • Lee C et al. (2012). Fasting cycles retard growth of tumors and sensitize a range of cancer cell types to chemotherapy. Sci Transl Med 4:124ra27.
  • Safdie FM et al. (2009). Fasting and cancer treatment in humans: a case series report. Aging 1:988–1007.
  • Dorff TB et al. (2016). Safety and feasibility of fasting in combination with platinum-based chemotherapy. BMC Cancer 16:360.
  • de Groot S et al. (2020). Fasting mimicking diet as an adjunct to neoadjuvant chemotherapy for breast cancer in the multicentre randomized phase 2 DIRECT trial. Nat Commun 11:3083.
  • Obrist F et al. (2018). Metabolic vulnerability of cisplatin-resistant cancers. EMBO J 37:e98597.
  • Fearon K et al. (2011). Definition and classification of cancer cachexia: an international consensus. Lancet Oncol 12:489–495.
  • de Pillis LG, Radunskaya AE (2001). A mathematical tumor model with immune resistance and drug therapy: an optimal control approach. J Theor Med 3:79–100 (values as tabulated in DTR-Bench, Luo et al. 2024, arXiv:2405.18610).
  • Feller C, Ebenbauer C (2017). Relaxed logarithmic barrier function based model predictive control of linear systems. IEEE Trans Autom Control 62:1223–1238.
  • Zhang J et al. (2017). Integrating evolutionary dynamics into treatment of metastatic castrate-resistant prostate cancer. Nat Commun 8:1816.
